transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Daniel Kim, Priya Nair, Marcus Liu, Hannah Ortiz (Redwood) / Rachel Gomez, Tom Becker, Dr. Elena Muir, Samir Khan (Everwell)

Summary: quick readout of the VPC QoS experiments, routing fallback behaviour during the surge test, and next steps to harden the runbook. Customer is leaning toward Private (VPC) deployment if we can show consistent p50/p95 under their traffic profile and a robust fallback to hosted models when on-prem capacity degrades.

Topics: QoS throttling results; KV cache warmup variability; routing policy thresholds; MTU/egress observations; controlled failover plan; security questions about logs and KMS isolation.

[00:00] Daniel Kim: hey everyone, thanks for making time, real quick agenda: results readout from last nights QoS sweep, then priya will walk through the fallback behaviour we saw in canary, then open Q/A and next steps.
[00:24] Rachel Gomez: thanks daniel, short on time here but we want the high level first — did you see the p95 blow up on the second run?
[00:34] Priya Nair: yeah so the second run had a traffic spike we didn't anticipate — there was a histogram shift toward longer seq lengths, about 30% more tokens on average which stressed the kv cache and increased tail latency. we saw p50 at 90ms but p95 jumped to 1.4s in the worst windows.
[01:05] Tom Becker: that 1.4s — was that network or the instance? i saw some packet drops on our end at the same timestamps.
[01:16] Hannah Ortiz: quick note, packet drops correlate with an MTU mismatch during the MTU change we pushed at 02:10 GMT; some flows were fragmented which caused extra retransmits. we still think most of the latency was kernel-level scheduling plus kv cache coldness, not pure network, but both added up.
[01:45] Dr. Elena Muir: when you say kv cache coldness, are you talking about prefix cache warming or the model kv cache? we need clarity because our prefixes are long.
[01:58] Priya Nair: good question — primarily model KV cache (the attention key/value store per token) plus prefix reuse. long prefixes reduce effective batching so you get worse tails if cache misses line up. also our batching heuristic right now uses a soft timeout which we tuned down to reduce latency but that can hurt efficiency.
[02:25] Samir Khan: is that the soft timeout we set to 8ms? i thought we moved to 5ms for this run.
[02:33] Priya Nair: right, we set soft timeout to 5ms and hard cap to 50ms. that helped p50 but under the worst-case long seq you still hit the tail.
[02:50] Rachel Gomez: ok so what's the mitigation path — can you force cache pinning or warm the kv ahead of time?
[03:00] Priya Nair: two approaches: 1) pre-warm using a synthetic prefix warming job (we can run during low traffic windows), 2) use smarter routing: route long-seq requests to a quantized variant with slightly higher throughput and lower per-token latency. tradeoff is quality delta — that's where the evals we asked for come in.
[03:25] Daniel Kim: let me add, we can also set a dynamic fallback policy: if p95 exceeds threshold for X seconds, route new requests to hosted fallback model with 95% compatibility. that's in the runbook draft.
[03:41] Tom Becker: hosted fallback — any data residency concerns? logs etc?
[03:47] Marcus Liu: we only send minimal request metadata for routing. payloads can be stripped or hashed; we also support E2E encryption and KMS key control on the VPC side so the customer retains key custody — doc will specify.
[04:05] Rachel Gomez: we need to see that in writing, especially around audit logs and retention.
[04:12] Daniel Kim: yes we'll add an appendix about log redaction, retention windows, and HSM/KMS integration.

--- Summary of last nights QoS sweep ---
[04:30] Priya Nair: ok i'll read the results: three runs, baseline, spike A, spike B. Baseline p50 82ms, p95 160ms. Spike A (moderate seq increase) p50 105ms p95 420ms. Spike B (long seq + MTU event) p50 90ms p95 1.4s. CPU/GPU metrics show higher host CPU uWait during spike B coincident with retransmits.
[05:10] Tom Becker: retransmits on which segment? i still think our firewall rules were kicking in for ephemeral ports.
[05:18] Hannah Ortiz: firewall logs show occasional late SYN/ACKs but the majority of packet errors were due to fragmentation; once we reverted MTU to original it improved. we recommend a maintenance window for MTU changes and a pre-check script which we'll provide.
[05:39] Dr. Elena Muir: can the pre-check script be run from our CI? we want something we can integrate.
[05:45] Hannah Ortiz: yes it's just an SSH/TCP/MTU probe plus a validation step for path MTU — we'll upload a small repo link.

[06:00] [Speaker 1]: i also want to highlight that the KV cache decay setting we used was conservative — 2000 token window — we can try increasing to 4000 to keep keys hot longer but memory footprint rises.
[06:17] Priya Nair: exactly, and that hits the tradeoff between RAM and latency. for your hardware profile we recommended a medium delta, but if you have spare memory we can bump.
[06:32] Samir Khan: how much extra memory? 10%? 20%?
[06:37] Priya Nair: typically +12-18% depending on quantization. we'll include numbers in the sheet.

[07:00] Daniel Kim: switching to routing/fallback behaviour from the canary where we simulated node failure — priya?
[07:07] Priya Nair: in the canary we took one on-prem GPU pool down. requests were routed according to policy: first attempt local, second attempt cross-pool, third attempt hosted fallback. we observed about 30s of elevated errors while routing table converged and then a steady routed-to-hosted of about 12% during the outage window. fallbacks served slightly older model variant but within our quality thresholds.
[07:45] Rachel Gomez: 30s of elevated errors is a lot for us; our SLAs expect under 10s.
[07:53] Priya Nair: understood. that window corresponds to the route re-eval and health-check interval which we can tune: reduce probe interval, aggressive circuit breaker, and pre-warming a standby on hosted for instant failover. each reduces error window but increases cost.
[08:12] Tom Becker: can you make the circuit breaker parameter visible in the console? we want to own the knob.
[08:18] Marcus Liu: yes the Redwood Console exposes those routing knobs per-deployment and we can give team-level RBAC to SREs. we'll show screen share later in demo if needed.

[08:36] [00:09:30] Rachel Gomez: quick interruption — security team asked about audit logs retention in hosted fallback flows. will hosted logs contain raw prompts?
[08:47] Daniel Kim: by default no, we hash prompts and store minimal metadata. customers can opt into full logs but that's disabled by default for privacy. if you need full logs we can set up a KMS-wrapped bucket.
[09:05] Dr. Elena Muir: how about SSO/SAML? we need enforced SSO for the console.
[09:12] Marcus Liu: Redwood supports SAML SSO with enforced MFA, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access. we'll send the SAML metadata and a short integration checklist.

--- Controlled failover proposal ---
[09:30] Priya Nair: proposal: 1) set p95 threshold to 600ms (adjustable), 2) grace period 15s, 3) circuit-breaker engages and sends new requests to hosted fallback, 4) background drain on on-prem pool and health-check retries to restore. also runbook will define manual override.
[10:02] Tom Becker: 15s is better than 30s but still double our desired target. can we reduce grace to 8s?
[10:11] Priya Nair: we can attempt 8s if you run a short failover test — the risk is flapping if probes are noisy. we suggest a test day.
[10:20] Rachel Gomez: schedule that test after we get the MTU pre-check and the traces to you.

[10:30] [00:11:00] Daniel Kim: switching to perf spreadsheet — priya will call out the important knobs.
[10:36] Priya Nair: knobs recap: soft batch timeout, hard batch cap, kv cache window, pre-warm job cadence, circuit breaker thresholds, routing priorities (local -> regional -> hosted), quantization profile for long-seq traffic. we attached a recommended baseline config for your guards.
[10:58] Samir Khan: quick question on quantization: did you see hallucination rates increase when you switched to the 4-bit quant?
[11:07] Priya Nair: small increase in rare tokens — we measured a 0.3% BLEU-ish delta on our eval set; user-visible hallucinations were minimal but depends on your dataset. if you have strict accuracy requirements, keep long-seq on the higher-precision variant.
[11:30] Dr. Elena Muir: can we run a targeted eval with our prompt set?
[11:34] Daniel Kim: yes that's one of the next steps — Samir you'll share the top prompts and we will run a compatibility eval and return a delta report.

[11:50] [00:12:30] Rachel Gomez: on legal/procurement — what would the pricing look like if we run with a standby hosted fallback continuously vs only on failover?
[11:58] Marcus Liu: we can model both. Standby reserved hosted capacity ~ fixed monthly plus small per-token. On-demand on failover is lower fixed cost but higher tail latency during cold start; we will include an economic comparison in the spreadsheet.
[12:20] Tom Becker: will that spreadsheet show per-token cost at p50 and p95? we need to budget for tail.
[12:27] Marcus Liu: yes per-token at p50/p95 and projected monthly cost for your traffic profile once you send traces.

[12:40] [00:13:10] Rachel Gomez: ok next — telemetry and alerting: our ops team wants >= 3 minute alerting for p95 violations and a webhook integration with PagerDuty.
[12:49] Hannah Ortiz: Console supports alerting rules and webhook endpoints; we can pre-configure a set of alerts for you and add the pagerduty integration. we'll also provide runbook templates for escalation.
[13:05] Samir Khan: can those alerts be per-route and token-class? we have embeddings traffic and text gen.
[13:12] Hannah Ortiz: yes, per-route and per-model variant, down to token classes if you tag them.

[13:30] [00:14:00] Rachel Gomez: anything surprising in your telemetry we should be aware of?
[13:36] Priya Nair: one oddity — we saw a small cluster of requests with anomalous cpu spikes that correlated with a particular prompt family that uses many function calls. we suspect a prompt engineering inefficiency causing repeated recursions.
[13:55] Dr. Elena Muir: that's likely from our inference enrichment process — we'll hunt that pattern on our side and remove the recursion.

[14:10] Daniel Kim: ok let's capture the immediate next steps and owners — i'm going to recap quickly.
[14:18] Daniel Kim: Redwood: share QoS perf sheet, fallback runbook v1, MTU pre-check repo, SAML metadata, and quantization/knob guide by 2027-01-21. Everwell: export traces, top prompts, schedule failover window 2027-01-26, validate MTU change window with ops.
[14:42] Rachel Gomez: yes, we'll get those to you. two asks — include a short section on audit-readiness and also a quick checklist for SOC2 auditors around access logs.
[14:54] Marcus Liu: we'll include SOC2 checklist and an appendix for auditors.

[15:05] [00:15:30] Tom Becker: small FYI: our SRE wants to change ephemeral port ranges to reduce NAT timeouts — that might improve retransmit behaviour. we'll notify you if that goes live.
[15:17] Hannah Ortiz: good to know — those changes can alter observed latency; we'll coordinate scheduling.

[15:30] Daniel Kim: any blockers from Everwell side that would prevent the 1/26 test?
[15:36] Rachel Gomez: only if we can't get the traces over by Friday the 22nd. otherwise green.
[15:41] Samir Khan: i'll prioritize the traces export.

[15:50] Daniel Kim: last item — small ask: do you want Redwood to run a blackbox synthetic load to validate the runbook once we've tuned the knobs?
[15:58] Rachel Gomez: yes, please run one before the 26th so we can see results together.
[16:04] Priya Nair: we'll schedule an internal run on the 23rd and share results.

[16:15] [00:16:45] Daniel Kim: all right thanks everyone — i'll send the notes and the action item list after this call. anything else?
[16:24] Dr. Elena Muir: thank you, helpful — please tag the runbook with our contact for incident drills.
[16:30] Daniel Kim: done. bye all.

End of transcript.

References shared during call: https://redwood.example.com/qos-perf-spreadsheet (doc), https://github.com/redwood/mtu-precheck (repo), runbook draft v1 (link to confluence)
